summary:
ANCASH DEPARTMENT STANDS UNDER THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK. No trans-specific regional ordinance, departmental decree or incident series for Ancash appears in the source inventory; every available item is national in scope, and the framework below is what a visitor to Ancash is scored against.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

In February 2025 the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting entry into public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than a person's birth sex, with narrow exceptions covering custody situations and cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argued the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

The plenary of Congress approved the fused text of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes on 2 April 2025 and waived a second vote; its Article 5.1 bars persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex, and the same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The same law's vague child-protection articles, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru read Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu, and found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people while implicitly framing them as harassment risks. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Enforcement reaches private life as well as state facilities. Consumer-protection body INDECOPI, in SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, presenter Ana Maria Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; among the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian, and 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women. Killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. The 2024 report's co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan Leon, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marin, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. The 2026 status of the bathroom restriction is unconfirmed in available sources, and no source in the inventory records any Ancash-specific enforcement action or incident.
tangentialFactors:
The bathroom regime is enforced through everyday private actors as well as public bodies, since venue staff and security are the ones who would check a DNI. A visitor should expect the restriction to surface at gyms, malls, transport hubs and hotels rather than only at government buildings.

The hate-crime vacuum places Peru alongside Paraguay and Guyana as the only South American states without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law, which affects how an assault would be classified and charged after the fact.

Speech risk is adjacent to facility risk. The April 2025 law's article 4 ban on media and advertising content and the raised obscenity sentence expose interpreters, guides, artists and hosts of events to child-protection framing, and Human Rights Watch describes child protection as a pretext for repression and scapegoating of trans people.

Comparative protections exist above the national level: Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights obliges states to guarantee trans people's full rights on the basis of protected personal autonomy, and the Azul Rojas Marin judgment is the regional court's first torture-by-discrimination case.

Recorded violence figures understate the picture. Killers went unidentified in 26 of 54 homicides between 2020 and 2023, and the state does not register sexual orientation or gender identity in its crime systems, so a visitor cannot rely on published counts as a measure of exposure.
localsOnly:
Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains a long, costly and invasive procedure, which shapes what documents residents carry and how a gender marker is recorded on the DNI used for bathroom and venue checks.

Residents face the April 2025 restriction on public sanitary facilities as law rather than proposal, with venue staff and security empowered to require a DNI check, and INDECOPI precedent in Resolution 0735-2022 signalling that complaints against private operators such as SmartFit can be dismissed.

Local LGBTI organisations work against a baseline of 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases recorded between 2020 and 2023 by the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia, with trans women the group most affected, and with official registration systems that do not capture orientation or gender identity.

Healthcare improved for residents in June 2024, when health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official guidance, a change described as a step toward dignity for trans patients.

Organising and public speech are constrained by the vague child-protection articles of the April 2025 law, including the article 4 ban on media and advertising content, and by the obscenity minimum sentence raised from three to four years. A constitutional court in Lima ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional in July 2025 after an activist legal challenge, which gives residents a domestic litigation route.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2026 status of the bathroom restriction, including any constitutional challenge to Article 5.1 or implementing regulation, is unconfirmed in available sources.

No departmental ordinance, municipal regulation or incident series specific to Ancash is present in the inventory; the absence of such material means Ancash-level enforcement practice is unresolved rather than known to be absent.

Whether public venues in Ancash actually apply DNI-based restroom checks in practice is not sourced; only the national rule and the documented SmartFit precedent are on record.

Hate-crime counts are a partial registry by the source's own account: Gianna Camacho states the figures are a sub-registry, and 26 of 54 homicides had no identified killer, so no reliable Ancash-level victim count exists.
